opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what you, as the founder, are not good at. A lot of first-time founders, especially those from technical or academic backgrounds like mine, build leadership teams in their own image: people who think the way they think and got excited about the same problems. That feels comfortable, but it creates blind spots.

So I'd say complementarity matters more than similarity. If the founder is deeply research-driven, you want someone on the leadership team who is obsessive about execution, about shipping and timelines. You also want someone who understands the business side, someone who can talk to customers and translate what the technology can do into something people will actually pay for.

At the same time, there has to be a shared core. Everyone needs to believe in the mission and agree on how hard and how fast you're willing to run. Complementary skills with misaligned values is a recipe for constant friction. The skills should be different, but the conviction should be the same.

The other thing I'd emphasize is talent density over title. Early on, it's tempting to hire someone with a big résumé from a large company and give them a VP title. But at a startup, leaders still need to be builders. They need to write the code, run the experiments, and sit in the customer meeting themselves. The best early leaders I've seen are people who could have been founders in their own right. They're mission-driven, they have high agency, and they don't need a large organization underneath them to be effective.

And finally, trust and speed of communication. A leadership team should be able to disagree openly, sometimes intensely, and then commit quickly. If people are being polite instead of being honest, you lose a lot of time. A small group of people who trust each other enough to argue, and then move as one, is a huge advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says complementarity matters more than similarity and warns against building a team in the founder’s image; it does not say team members should resemble the founder.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Facebook or employees’ identification with it.

fable-5.1.text:
When I think about building a leadership team, the first principle is honesty with yourself about what you are not. I came out of math and a research background. I know how to reason about hard problems and recruit people who want to work on hard problems. I did not come out with experience scaling an organization, running a sales motion, or managing a large engineering org through a crisis. So the team has to be composed around the founder's gaps, not around the founder's comfort.

The second thing is that at the very beginning, I don't actually think you should hire a "leadership team" in the traditional sense. Early on you want builders who can also lead, not managers who used to build. At Axiom, the people in the earliest layer were researchers and engineers who could sit down and produce the thing themselves, and who happened to have the judgment to grow a group under them later. If you hire a polished executive before there is anything for them to execute on, they get frustrated and the company gets heavier than it should be.

Third, I care a lot about a mix of what I'd call temperaments. You want at least one person who is deeply paranoid about what can go wrong, one person who is relentlessly optimistic about what the product can become, and someone who is obsessed with the customer rather than the technology. If everyone around the table is a technologist excited about the same ideas, you end up building something beautiful that nobody needs. In a company doing frontier AI for mathematics, that pull toward building for ourselves is very strong, so I deliberately counterbalance it.

Fourth, I look for people who have a track record of disagreeing with authority and still being trusted by it. The worst leadership teams are either a group of yes-people around a charismatic founder, or a group of strong egos who can't resolve conflict. What you want is people who will fight hard in the room and then genuinely commit once a decision is made. I probe for that in interviews: tell me about a time you thought your boss was wrong and what you did.

And the last point, which I think is underrated, is shared taste. Not shared background, shared taste. A mathematician, a systems engineer, and a go-to-market leader can come from completely different worlds, but they should all recognize the same thing as excellent and the same thing as sloppy. If taste is aligned, you can delegate much faster, because you don't have to inspect every decision. If it isn't, no amount of process will save you.

So in short: hire around your weaknesses, hire builders first, diversify temperament, select for principled disagreement, and insist on shared taste. The composition evolves as the company grows, but those filters have stayed constant for me.

r001.rationale: The response says to hire around the founder’s weaknesses and diversify temperaments and backgrounds. Shared taste is mentioned, but it does not state that team members should resemble the founder.

astra-6.text:
I think entrepreneurs should start by being honest about their own strengths and weaknesses. It’s tempting to hire people who think like you, because those conversations feel easy. But a leadership team needs people who see problems you miss and bring skills you don’t have.

I’d look for alignment on the mission and values, alongside differences in expertise and perspective. Can you disagree openly? Can someone tell you that your favorite idea isn’t working? And once you’ve made a decision, can everyone commit to executing it?

The composition also depends on the stage of the company. Early on, you need people who are comfortable with uncertainty and willing to do things outside their job descriptions. As you grow, you need more specialization. The key is to build the team around what the company needs next, while being clear about who owns each decision.

r001.rationale: The response favors complementary skills and perspectives; it does not say entrepreneurs need team members who resemble them beyond complementing them.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Facebook or employees’ identification with the company.

sol-6.1.text:
I think entrepreneurs should look for people who complement them, especially in areas where they’re less experienced. You don’t want a leadership team where everyone has the same strengths, the same background, and the same blind spots.

At the same time, you need alignment on the mission and on how you work together. People should be able to disagree openly, make a decision, and then commit to it. So I’d look for shared values, different perspectives, and clear ownership. And that composition will evolve: the leadership team you need to find your first customers may be different from the one you need to scale.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends people who complement the entrepreneur and have different perspectives; it does not say team members should resemble them.
